title: "Parameter estimation and confidence intervals"
---

```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 5, dpi = 110)
library(RColorBrewer)
pal <- brewer.pal(8, "Paired")
set.seed(40)
```

*Session 6 of the [course](index.html) · [Slides for this session (PDF)](slides/06-parameter-estimation.pdf)*

**Learning goals.** After this lesson you can

- explain what "95% confidence" refers to, and what it does not refer to;
- compute a confidence interval for a mean by hand and with `t.test()`;
- describe how the sample size and the confidence level change the width of an
  interval.

## The question

We almost never know a population mean. We take one sample, compute its mean,
and want to say how far that estimate might be from the truth. A confidence
interval is a range of plausible values. But what exactly is "95%" about it?

The answer is easiest to *see*. In a simulation we can do what is impossible in
real research: fix the true population mean, and then draw many samples from
the population.

## An experiment with repeated sampling

The population is normal with mean $\mu = 40$ and standard deviation
$\sigma = 2$. We draw a sample of $n = 20$, compute the 95% confidence interval

$$\bar{x} \pm z_{0.975} \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}},$$

and repeat this 100 times. Each horizontal line below is one interval. Intervals
that cover the true mean are green; intervals that miss it are red.

```{r coverage, fig.height = 6}
mu <- 40; sigma <- 2; n <- 20
repeats <- 100
conf_level <- 0.95
z <- qnorm(1 - (1 - conf_level) / 2)

lower <- upper <- numeric(repeats)
for (i in 1:repeats) {
  x <- rnorm(n, mu, sigma)
  margin <- z * sigma / sqrt(n)
  lower[i] <- mean(x) - margin
  upper[i] <- mean(x) + margin
}
covers <- lower <= mu & upper >= mu

plot(NULL, xlim = range(lower, upper), ylim = c(1, repeats),
     xlab = "Value", ylab = "Sample number",
     main = paste0(sum(covers), " of ", repeats, " intervals cover the true mean"))
segments(lower, 1:repeats, upper, 1:repeats, lwd = 2,
         col = ifelse(covers, pal[4], pal[6]))
abline(v = mu, lwd = 2, lty = 2)
```

```{r coverage-rate}
mean(covers)
```

Run the chunk again and the picture changes, but the proportion of intervals
that cover the true mean stays close to 95%. That is what the confidence level
describes: **the long-run proportion of intervals, produced by this procedure,
that contain the true value.** Any single interval either contains $\mu$ or it
does not; we just cannot tell which.

With many more repetitions the coverage rate gets very close to the nominal
level:

```{r coverage-many}
coverage <- function(n, conf_level, repeats = 10000) {
  z <- qnorm(1 - (1 - conf_level) / 2)
  means <- replicate(repeats, mean(rnorm(n, mu, sigma)))
  mean(abs(means - mu) <= z * sigma / sqrt(n))
}
coverage(n = 20, conf_level = 0.95)
coverage(n = 20, conf_level = 0.90)
```

## When the population standard deviation is unknown: the t interval

In practice we do not know $\sigma$ and estimate it with the sample standard
deviation $s$. The extra uncertainty is handled by using the $t$ distribution,
which has heavier tails than the normal distribution, especially for small
samples:

```{r t-dist}
x <- seq(-4, 4, 0.01)
plot(x, dnorm(x), type = "l", lwd = 2, col = "red", ylab = "Density", xlab = "")
for (k in 1:3) lines(x, dt(x, df = c(2, 5, 20)[k]), lwd = 2, col = pal[2 * k])
legend("topright", legend = c("N(0, 1)", "t (df = 2)", "t (df = 5)", "t (df = 20)"),
       col = c("red", pal[c(2, 4, 6)]), lwd = 2, bty = "n")
```

The interval becomes $\bar{x} \pm t_{0.975,\,n-1}\, s/\sqrt{n}$. By hand and with
`t.test()`:

```{r t-interval}
x <- rnorm(20, mu, sigma)
mean(x) + c(-1, 1) * qt(0.975, df = 19) * sd(x) / sqrt(20)
t.test(x, conf.level = 0.95)$conf.int
```

## What makes an interval wider or narrower?

```{r width}
width <- function(n, conf_level) 2 * qnorm(1 - (1 - conf_level) / 2) * sigma / sqrt(n)
ns <- c(10, 20, 50, 100, 200, 500)
plot(ns, width(ns, 0.95), type = "b", pch = 19, col = pal[2], log = "x",
     xlab = "Sample size (log scale)", ylab = "Interval width",
     ylim = c(0, max(width(ns, 0.99))))
lines(ns, width(ns, 0.90), type = "b", pch = 19, col = pal[4])
lines(ns, width(ns, 0.99), type = "b", pch = 19, col = pal[6])
legend("topright", legend = c("90%", "95%", "99%"), col = pal[c(4, 2, 6)],
       pch = 19, bty = "n", title = "Confidence level")
```

Larger samples give narrower intervals: the width shrinks with $1/\sqrt{n}$, so
halving the width requires four times as many observations. A higher
confidence level gives wider intervals: more certainty that the procedure
captures $\mu$ costs precision.

## Try it yourself

1. Change `conf_level` in the first simulation to 0.80. Roughly how many of the
   100 intervals should miss the true mean? Check.
2. Draw the samples from a skewed population instead, for example
   `rexp(n, rate = 1/40)` (mean 40), and estimate the coverage of the t
   interval for $n = 5$, $n = 20$ and $n = 100$. What do you notice, and how
   does it relate to the central limit theorem from the lesson on probability and simulation?
3. A newspaper reports: "there is a 95% probability that the true mean lies
   between 38.9 and 41.2." Using the simulation, explain what is imprecise
   about this sentence.
